claim: MprF is the synthase and flippase of the phospholipid lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol.
source: Multiple peptide resistance factor (MprF) is the synthase and flippase of the phospholipid lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol that increases virulence and resistance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and other pathogens to cationic host defense peptides and antibiotics.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of MprF, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: MprF increases virulence and resistance of MRSA to cationic host defense peptides and antibiotics.
source: Multiple peptide resistance factor (MprF) is the synthase and flippase of the phospholipid lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol that increases virulence and resistance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and other pathogens to cationic host defense peptides and antibiotics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Antibody M-C7.1 targets a specific loop in the flippase domain of MprF.
source: Antibody M-C7.1 targeted a specific loop in the flippase domain that proved to be exposed at both sides of the bacterial membrane, thereby enhancing the mechanistic understanding of bacterial lipid translocation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including binding assays and SCAM analysis.

claim: The MprF loop targeted by M-C7.1 is exposed at both sides of the bacterial membrane.
source: Antibody M-C7.1 targeted a specific loop in the flippase domain that proved to be exposed at both sides of the bacterial membrane, thereby enhancing the mechanistic understanding of bacterial lipid translocation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SCAM experiments shown in Figure 2B and discussed in the results.

claim: M-C7.1 renders MRSA susceptible to host antimicrobial peptides.
source: M-C7.1 rendered MRSA susceptible to host antimicrobial peptides and antibiotics such as daptomycin, and it impaired MRSA survival in human phagocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: M-C7.1 renders MRSA susceptible to daptomycin.
source: M-C7.1 rendered MRSA susceptible to host antimicrobial peptides and antibiotics such as daptomycin, and it impaired MRSA survival in human phagocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: M-C7.1 impairs MRSA survival in human phagocytes.
source: M-C7.1 rendered MRSA susceptible to host antimicrobial peptides and antibiotics such as daptomycin, and it impaired MRSA survival in human phagocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Antibiotic resistance rates are continuously increasing.
source: The continuous increase of antibiotic resistance rates undermines the significance and efficacy of available antibiotics against bacterial infections (Årdal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Årdal et al., 2020.

claim: MRSA is responsible for a large percentage of superficial and severe bacterial infections.
source: MRSA is responsible for a large percentage of superficial and severe bacterial infections and the available last-resort antibiotics are much less effective than beta-lactams (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: No new class of antibiotics has entered the clinical phase since the introduction of daptomycin in 2003.
source: Unfortunately, no new class of antibiotics has entered the clinical phase since the introduction of the lipopeptide antibiotic daptomycin in 2003 (Årdal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Årdal et al., 2020.

claim: MprF is crucial for the capacity of bacterial pathogens to resist cationic antimicrobial peptides.
source: The multiple peptide resistance factor (MprF), a large integral membrane protein, is crucial for the capacity of bacterial pathogens such as S. aureus to resist cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) of the innate immune system and CAMP-like antibiotics such as daptomycin (Peschel et al., 2001; Ernst and Peschel, 2011; Slavetinsky et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Peschel et al., 2001; Ernst and Peschel, 2011; Slavetinsky et al., 2017).

claim: MprF is highly conserved and can be found in various Gram-positive or Gram-negative pathogens.
source: MprF is highly conserved and can be found in various Gram-positive or Gram-negative pathogens (Slavetinsky et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Slavetinsky et al., 2017.

claim: MprF proteins are crucial for in vivo virulence of various pathogens in infection models.
source: MprF proteins proved to be crucial for in vivo virulence of various pathogens in infection models (Peschel et al., 2001; Thedieck et al., 2006; Maloney et al., 2009) and when exposed to human phagocytes as a result of increased resistance to phagocyte-derived antimicrobial agents such as CAMPs (Slavetinsky et al., 2017; Kristian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Peschel et al., 2001; Thedieck et al., 2006; Maloney et al., 2009; Slavetinsky et al., 2017; Kristian et al., 2003).

claim: MprF forms oligomers.
source: MprF forms oligomers and it is a bifunctional enzyme, which can be separated into two distinct domains (Ernst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2015.

claim: MprF is a bifunctional enzyme with two distinct domains.
source: MprF forms oligomers and it is a bifunctional enzyme, which can be separated into two distinct domains (Ernst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2015.

claim: The C-terminal domain of MprF synthesizes lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol from phosphatidylglycerol and Lys-tRNA.
source: The C-terminal domain synthesizes positively charged lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (LysPG) from a negatively charged phosphatidylglycerol (PG) acceptor and a Lys-tRNA donor substrate, while the N-terminal domain translocates newly synthesized LysPG from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane and thus functions as a phospholipid flippase (Ernst et al., 2009; Roy and Ibba, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: The N-terminal domain of MprF translocates LysPG from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: The C-terminal domain synthesizes positively charged lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (LysPG) from a negatively charged phosphatidylglycerol (PG) acceptor and a Lys-tRNA donor substrate, while the N-terminal domain translocates newly synthesized LysPG from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane and thus functions as a phospholipid flippase (Ernst et al., 2009; Roy and Ibba, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: The N-terminal domain of MprF functions as a phospholipid flippase.
source: The C-terminal domain synthesizes positively charged lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (LysPG) from a negatively charged phosphatidylglycerol (PG) acceptor and a Lys-tRNA donor substrate, while the N-terminal domain translocates newly synthesized LysPG from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane and thus functions as a phospholipid flippase (Ernst et al., 2009; Roy and Ibba, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: The exposure of LysPG at the outer surface of the membrane reduces the affinity for CAMPs and other antimicrobials.
source: The exposure of LysPG at the outer surface of the membrane reduces the affinity for CAMPs and other antimicrobials (Ernst et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2009.

claim: mprF is a major hot spot for gain-of-function point mutations that lead to daptomycin resistance.
source: Notably, mprF is a major hot spot for gain-of-function point mutations that lead to daptomycin resistance, acquired during therapy of S. aureus infections (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2018.

claim: The hydrophobic part of S. aureus MprF appears to include 14 transmembrane segments.
source: The hydrophobic part of S. aureus MprF appears to include 14 TMS connected by loops with predicted lengths between 2 and 56 amino acids (Ernst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2015.

claim: Several loops of MprF are located at the outer surface of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Several of the loops are located at the outer surface of the cytoplasmic membrane, accessible to mABs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Antibodies M-C1, M-C7.1, M-C7.3, M-C9.1, M-C13.1, and M-C13.2 bound significantly stronger to MprF-expressing S. aureus compared to MprF-deficient S. aureus.
source: Antibodies M-C1, M-C7.1, M-C7.3, M-C9.1, M-C13.1, and M-C13.2 bound significantly stronger to MprF-expressing S. aureus (SA113Δspa) compared to MprF-deficient S. aureus (SA113ΔspaΔmprF), while the humanized isotype control mAB L-1 showed no specific binding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The isotype control mAB L-1 showed no specific binding to S. aureus.
source: Antibodies M-C1, M-C7.1, M-C7.3, M-C9.1, M-C13.1, and M-C13.2 bound significantly stronger to MprF-expressing S. aureus (SA113Δspa) compared to MprF-deficient S. aureus (SA113ΔspaΔmprF), while the humanized isotype control mAB L-1 showed no specific binding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loop 7 of MprF is accessible from the outside of the bacterial membrane.
source: Of note, loop 7 between potential TMS 7 and 8 whose location had previously remained controversial was detected by antibodies M-C7.1 and M-C7.3 (Figure 1B) indicating that loop 7 is accessible from the outside.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: M-C7.1 binds to MprF in live S. aureus cells.
source: S. aureus cells expressing either unmodified MprF or MprF-GFP yielded a protein band migrating at a molecular weight of around 900 kDa when preincubated with M-C7.1 but not with L-1 or in cells with the empty-vector control (pRB) (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: M-C7.1 forms a complex with MprF that migrates at approximately 900 kDa.
source: The 900 kDa bands probably represent a complex formed by MprF and M-C7.1, which confirms that M-C7.1 specifically binds MprF loop seven in live S. aureus cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MprF loop 7 was found at both the inner and outer surface of the membrane.
source: Notably, MprF loop 7 was found in both locations, at the inner and outer surface of the membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by SCAM experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loop 7 of MprF may have some degree of mobility in the membrane.
source: This finding corroborates the ambiguous position of loop 7 and suggests that this loop may have some degree of mobility in the membrane, which may reflect the lipid translocation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the SCAM data showing loop 7 at both membrane surfaces.

claim: mABs M-C7.1 and M-C13.1 increased the sensitivity of S. aureus SA113Δspa to nisin.
source: Two of the MprF-specific mABs targeting loops 7 or 13 increased the sensitivity of S. aureus SA113Δspa to nisin while the other mABs and the isotype control mAB L-1 had no significant impact (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mAB M-C7.1 caused the strongest sensitization to nisin.
source: mAB M-C7.1 caused the strongest sensitization (Figure 3A) and it synergized with nisin in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: M-C7.1 synergizes with nisin in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: mAB M-C7.1 caused the strongest sensitization (Figure 3A) and it synergized with nisin in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: M-C7.1 increases the susceptibility of USA300 to the human CAMP LL-37.
source: M-C7.1 was found to also increase the susceptibility of USA300 WT to the human CAMP LL-37, a host defense peptide produced by epithelial and phagocyte cells (Pinheiro da Silva and Machado, 2017), and to daptomycin, a lipopeptide antibiotic in clinical use sharing physicochemical and antibacterial properties with CAMPs (Bayer et al., 2013), in addition to nisin (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: M-C7.1 increases the antimicrobial activity of daptomycin against daptomycin-resistant CA-MRSA isolate 703.
source: M-C7.1 also increased the antimicrobial activity of daptomycin against the daptomycin-resistant (DAP-R) clinical CA-MRSA isolate 703 possessing the gain-of-function mutation S295L in MprF (Jones et al., 2008; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: M-C7.1 can reduce daptomycin MIC of both S. aureus SA113 WT and the DAP-R strain 703.
source: Of note, M-C7.1 could reduce daptomycin minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of both, S. aureus SA113 WT and the DAP-R strain 703 (Figure 3F), suggesting that M-C7.1 may potentially be able to overcome daptomycin resistance during therapy.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: M-C7.1 may potentially be able to overcome daptomycin resistance during therapy.
source: Of note, M-C7.1 could reduce daptomycin minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of both, S. aureus SA113 WT and the DAP-R strain 703 (Figure 3F), suggesting that M-C7.1 may potentially be able to overcome daptomycin resistance during therapy.
evidence: This is speculated based on the MIC reduction data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: M-C7.1 can inhibit growth of USA300 WT in the presence of subinhibitory concentrations of nisin.
source: M-C7.1 but not the isotype control mAB L-1 was able to inhibit growth of USA300 WT in the presence of subinhibitory concentrations of nisin (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The MprF segment targeted by M-C7.1 is not prone to quickly occurring escape mutations.
source: When USA300 WT was passaged for several days through media with M-C7.1 at 10 or 100 nM and with or without subinhibitory daptomycin (0.5 µg/ml), no point mutations in mprF were found suggesting that the MprF segment targeted by M-C7.1 is not prone to quickly occurring escape mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that no mutations were found after passaging.

claim: M-C7.1 binds MprF at the junction between the LysPG synthase and flippase domains.
source: M-C7.1 binds MprF at the junction between the LysPG synthase and flippase domains (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The synthase function of MprF is not inhibited by M-C7.1.
source: The lipid patterns of SA113 WT treated with M-C7.1 at concentrations that increased the susceptibility to nisin or with the isotype control mAB L-1 were compared but showed no differences indicating that the synthase function of MprF was not inhibited by M-C7.1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment of SA113 WT with M-C7.1 leads to a significant increase in the capacity to bind cytochrome C.
source: Treatment of SA113 WT with M-C7.1 at concentrations that increased the susceptibility to nisin led to a significant increase in the capacity to bind cytochrome C or annexin V compared to SA113 WT without treatment or treated with isotype control mAB L-1 (Figure 4B, C) thereby indicating that M-C7.1 inhibits the flippase function of MprF.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment of SA113 WT with M-C7.1 leads to a significant increase in the capacity to bind annexin V.
source: Treatment of SA113 WT with M-C7.1 at concentrations that increased the susceptibility to nisin led to a significant increase in the capacity to bind cytochrome C or annexin V compared to SA113 WT without treatment or treated with isotype control mAB L-1 (Figure 4B, C) thereby indicating that M-C7.1 inhibits the flippase function of MprF.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: M-C7.1 inhibits the flippase function of MprF.
source: Treatment of SA113 WT with M-C7.1 at concentrations that increased the susceptibility to nisin led to a significant increase in the capacity to bind cytochrome C or annexin V compared to SA113 WT without treatment or treated with isotype control mAB L-1 (Figure 4B, C) thereby indicating that M-C7.1 inhibits the flippase function of MprF.
evidence: This is inferred from the cytochrome C and annexin V binding data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The protein region of MprF loop 7 and adjacent TMSs may accomplish a crucial function in the process of phospholipid translocation.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the protein region of MprF loop 7 and adjacent TMSs may accomplish a crucial function in the process of phospholipid translocation, as suggested by the dynamic localization of loop 7 on the cytoplasmic and external faces of the membrane.
evidence: This is speculated based on the dynamic localization of loop 7 observed in the SCAM experiments.

claim: S. aureus mprF mutants are more susceptible to PMN killing than the parental strains.
source: Accordingly, S. aureus mprF mutants are more susceptible to PMN killing than the parental strains while their opsonization and phagocytosis by PMNs remains unaltered (Peschel et al., 2001; Kristian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peschel et al., 2001 and Kristian et al., 2003.

claim: Treatment with M-C7.1 or the isotype control mAB L-1 did not alter the rate of PMN phagocytosis.
source: Treatment with M-C7.1 or the isotype control mAB L-1 did not alter the rate of PMN phagocytosis, but M-C7.1-treated USA300 cells were significantly more rapidly killed by PMNs than those treated with the isotype control antibody (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: M-C7.1-treated USA300 cells were significantly more rapidly killed by PMNs than those treated with the isotype control antibody.
source: Treatment with M-C7.1 or the isotype control mAB L-1 did not alter the rate of PMN phagocytosis, but M-C7.1-treated USA300 cells were significantly more rapidly killed by PMNs than those treated with the isotype control antibody (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: S. aureus treatment with M-C7.1 might reduce the capacity to persist in infections.
source: Thus, S. aureus treatment with M-C7.1 might reduce the capacity to persist in infections and may help to blunt the virulence of S. aureus in invasive infections.
evidence: This is speculated based on the PMN killing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: M-C7.1 may help to blunt the virulence of S. aureus in invasive infections.
source: Thus, S. aureus treatment with M-C7.1 might reduce the capacity to persist in infections and may help to blunt the virulence of S. aureus in invasive infections.
evidence: This is speculated based on the PMN killing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Therapeutic mABs have proven efficacy for neutralization of bacterial toxins.
source: Monoclonal therapeutic antibodies have proven efficacy for neutralization of bacterial toxins such as Clostridium botulinum or Clostridioides difficile toxins, and mAB-based therapies targeting the S. aureus alpha toxins and leukotoxins are currently developed (Dickey et al., 2017; Tabor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dickey et al., 2017 and Tabor et al., 2016.

claim: mABs inhibiting crucial cellular mechanisms of bacterial pathogens have hardly been assessed so far.
source: In contrast, mABs inhibiting crucial cellular mechanisms of bacterial pathogens have hardly been assessed so far (Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: The inhibition of MprF by M-C7.1 sensitized S. aureus to CAMPs and daptomycin.
source: However, the inhibition of MprF by M-C7.1 sensitized S. aureus to CAMPs and daptomycin and promoted killing by human PMNs, which use CAMPs as an important component of their antimicrobial arsenal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The inhibition of MprF by M-C7.1 promoted killing by human PMNs.
source: However, the inhibition of MprF by M-C7.1 sensitized S. aureus to CAMPs and daptomycin and promoted killing by human PMNs, which use CAMPs as an important component of their antimicrobial arsenal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Specific inhibition of MprF could promote the capacity of human host defense to clear or prevent a S. aureus infection.
source: Specific inhibition of MprF could therefore promote the capacity of human host defense to clear or prevent a S. aureus infection and would, at the same time, increase the susceptibility of S. aureus to CAMP-like antibiotics such as daptomycin.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing increased susceptibility to CAMPs and PMN killing.

claim: Specific inhibition of MprF would increase the susceptibility of S. aureus to CAMP-like antibiotics such as daptomycin.
source: Specific inhibition of MprF could therefore promote the capacity of human host defense to clear or prevent a S. aureus infection and would, at the same time, increase the susceptibility of S. aureus to CAMP-like antibiotics such as daptomycin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The capacity of antibodies to traverse the cell wall and reach the cytoplasmic membrane of S. aureus has remained controversial.
source: The capacity of antibodies to traverse the cell wall and reach the cytoplasmic membrane of S. aureus has remained controversial (Reichmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reichmann et al., 2014.

claim: Specific antibodies can reach membrane-associated epitopes in S. aureus.
source: However, other labs' and our findings demonstrate that specific antibodies can reach membrane-associated epitopes in S. aureus (Mishra et al., 2012; Weisman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mishra et al., 2012 and Weisman et al., 2009, and by the current study's findings.

claim: A recent atomic-force microscopy-based study revealed large, irregular pores in the cell wall of S. aureus.
source: A recent atomic-force microscopy-based study revealed large, irregular pores in the cell wall of S. aureus, which might allow large proteins such as antibodies to reach the cytoplasmic membrane (Pasquina-Lemonche et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pasquina-Lemonche et al., 2020.

claim: M-C7.1 sensitizes S. aureus in the presence of protein A.
source: M-C7.1 sensitized S. aureus also in the presence of protein A indicating that the unspecific IgG binding by protein A does not interfere with the M-C7.1 capacity to block MprF.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments using wild-type strains with intact protein A.

claim: Specific binding of MprF antibody M-C7.1 to the extracellular loop 7 inhibited the flippase function of MprF.
source: Specific binding of MprF antibody M-C7.1 to the extracellular loop 7 inhibited the flippase function of MprF, which indicates that this loop plays a crucial role in the lipid translocation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the flippase inhibition data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loop 7 of MprF plays a crucial role in the lipid translocation process.
source: Specific binding of MprF antibody M-C7.1 to the extracellular loop 7 inhibited the flippase function of MprF, which indicates that this loop plays a crucial role in the lipid translocation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the flippase inhibition data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The protein part formed by loop 7 and adjacent TMS 7 and 8 may change its position in the protein complex, moving between the two membrane surfaces to accomplish LysPG translocation.
source: This suggests that the protein part formed by loop 7 and adjacent TMS 7 and 8 may change its position in the protein complex, moving between the two membrane surfaces to accomplish LysPG translocation (Figure 6), or it could be in a unique position of the large MprF protein complex that allows access from both sides.
evidence: This is speculated based on the SCAM data showing loop 7 at both membrane surfaces.

claim: The protein part formed by loop 7 and adjacent TMS 7 and 8 could be in a unique position of the large MprF protein complex that allows access from both sides.
source: This suggests that the protein part formed by loop 7 and adjacent TMS 7 and 8 may change its position in the protein complex, moving between the two membrane surfaces to accomplish LysPG translocation (Figure 6), or it could be in a unique position of the large MprF protein complex that allows access from both sides.
evidence: This is speculated based on the SCAM data showing loop 7 at both membrane surfaces.

claim: The protein part formed by loop 7 and adjacent TMS might represent the center of the MprF flippase.
source: This protein part might represent the center of the MprF flippase establishing the previously reported MprF-dependent distribution of charged LysPG in the inner and outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane of S. aureus (Ernst et al., 2009; Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculated based on the SCAM data and previous findings cited from Ernst et al., 2009.

claim: The three-dimensional structure of the MprF protein of Rhizobium tropici was reported.
source: While this manuscript was in revision, the three-dimensional structure of the MprF protein of Rhizobium tropici was reported.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The region corresponding to the S. aureus MprF loop 7 is part of a gate between two large protein cavities in the Rhizobium tropici MprF structure.
source: It demonstrates that the region corresponding to the S. aureus MprF loop 7 is part of a gate between two large protein cavities, which are accessible from the outer and inner surface of the cytoplasmic membrane and allow for the passage of LysPG molecules between the two membrane leaflets (Song et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2021.

claim: Song et al. suggest a mechanistic model where LysPG binding in the inner protein cavity of the MprF flippase results in a transient channel formation/gate opening.
source: Song et al. suggest a mechanistic model where LysPG binding in the inner protein cavity of the MprF flippase results in a transient channel formation/gate opening allowing LysPG to diffuse into the outer protein cavity which would put the M-C7.1-binding site in the center of the flipping process.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanistic model proposed by Song et al. would explain why M-C7.1 binding to MprF seems to require the live S. aureus cell to achieve structural accessibility to MprF.
source: This model would explain why M-C7.1 binding to MprF seems to require the live S. aureus cell to achieve structural accessibility to MprF.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data from Song et al., 2021 and the current study's findings.

claim: Song et al. confirmed that MprF forms homodimers and larger oligomers.
source: Moreover, Song et al. confirmed that MprF forms homodimers and larger oligomers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2021.

claim: Replacement of conserved amino acids in the M-C7.1-targeted protein part has been shown to inhibit the flippase function of MprF.
source: Replacement of conserved amino acids in the M-C7.1-targeted protein part has been shown to inhibit the flippase function of MprF (Ernst et al., 2015), which underscores the crucial function of this domain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2015.

claim: One of the conserved and essential amino acids in TMS 7, D254, is negatively charged.
source: Notably, one of the conserved and essential amino acids in TMS 7, D254, is negatively charged.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: D254 may interact with the positively charged head group of LysPG during the translocation process in the S. aureus MprF.
source: It is tempting to speculate that D254 may interact with the positively charged head group of LysPG during the translocation process in the S. aureus MprF.
evidence: This is speculated based on the chemical properties of D254 and LysPG.

claim: Mutations on loop 7 and adjacent TMS have been found to cause specific resistance to daptomycin and friulimicin B but not to other antimicrobials.
source: Mutations on loop 7 and adjacent TMS have recently been found to cause specific resistance to the structurally related lipopeptide antibiotics daptomycin and friulimicin B but not to other antimicrobials (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations on loop 7 and adjacent TMS allow the flippase to translocate lipopeptide antibiotics instead of or together with LysPG.
source: Indirect evidence has suggested that these mutations allow the flippase to translocate these lipopeptide antibiotics instead of or together with LysPG (Ernst et al., 2018), which is in agreement with a direct role of loop 7 in the translocation process.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2018.

claim: A mAB-binding loop 13 also sensitized S. aureus to nisin in a similar but less pronounced way as M-C7.1.
source: A mAB-binding loop 13 also sensitized S. aureus to nisin in a similar but less pronounced way as M-C7.1 suggesting that this loop may also have a critical role for MprF activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loop 13 may have a critical role for MprF activity.
source: A mAB-binding loop 13 also sensitized S. aureus to nisin in a similar but less pronounced way as M-C7.1 suggesting that this loop may also have a critical role for MprF activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the nisin sensitization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MprF has the advantage that essential parts of it are exposed at the external surface of the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Compared to other potential targets, MprF has the advantage that essential parts of it are exposed at the external surface of the cytoplasmic membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by the experimental findings.

claim: MprF is found in many other bacterial pathogens.
source: Moreover, MprF is found in many other bacterial pathogens for which similar therapeutic mABs could be developed (Ernst et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ernst et al., 2009.

claim: Only a few amino acids in loop 7 are conserved in other bacteria.
source: On the other hand, only a few amino acids in loop 7 are conserved in other bacteria, which would limit the impact of loop-7-directed mABs on other microbiome members thereby minimizing the resistance selection pressure and the risk of dysbiosis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The limited conservation of loop 7 amino acids would minimize the resistance selection pressure and the risk of dysbiosis from loop-7-directed mABs.
source: On the other hand, only a few amino acids in loop 7 are conserved in other bacteria, which would limit the impact of loop-7-directed mABs on other microbiome members thereby minimizing the resistance selection pressure and the risk of dysbiosis.

claim: The cysteine-deficient MprF mutant protein decreases the susceptibility of the S. aureus mprF mutant to daptomycin.
